Thursday, November 05, 2026 EID Journal: Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 #19,402 In the spring of 2024 a mysterious illness spreading among Texas, Kansas, and New Mexico dairy cattle was identified as avian H5N1, an outbreak that has now spread to at least 21 states, and has affected > 1200 herds. At that time cattle were believed poorly susceptible to influenza A (see A Brief History Of Influenza A In Cattle/Ruminants), and so testing for H5N1 was delayed. The immediate global reaction was that this was an `American problem', caused by a new (and presumably unique to North America) strain (B3.13) of H5N1 (see DEFRA Risk Assessment Of HPAI H5N1 Occurring in Cattle In the UK), and unlikely to occur in Europe. This strain has not been detected in the UK, and none of the viruses detected in the UK over the 2020 to 2024 HPAI outbreak period have contained genetic material originating from North or South American viruses. The risk to GB of H5N1 in livestock is assessed at very low. That assumption was challenged in June of 2024 (see Germany: FLI Statement On Experimental Infection Of Dairy Cows With European H5N1 Virus) when researchers demonstrated that a German virus isolate could replicate in a cow's udder after experimental infection. Over the summer of 2024 the USDA reassuringly suggested that B3.13 entered dairy cattle via a single spillover from birds - and was subsequently spread by the interstate transport of infected dairy cows. That assumption held until early 2025 when another genotype (D1.1) turned up in dairy cattle in two states (Nevada & Arizona). In March of 2025, the UK's Defra reported H5N1 Detected In Domestic Sheep with Mastitis, and over the previous year we'd seen reports of other non-B3.13 H5N1 in goats and sheep in Pakistan, horses in Mongolia, and pigs in Oregon. Also in the spring of 2025, Chinese scientists warned that Clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1 influenza Viruses from Birds in China Replicated Effectively in Bovine cells. Last April, in Preprint: Infection of the Bovine Mammary Gland by Avian H5N1 Subclade 2.3.4.4b Influenza viruses. we saw even more evidence that diverse HPAI H5 strains could infect dairy cattle. The authors wrote: Our findings show that mammary tissue from common cattle breeds is permissive to clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection. These results support the view that bovine mammary epithelium represents a susceptible tissue environment and suggest that IAV infection in cattle may be more widespread than previously assumed. Four months ago, in Eurosurveillance: Detection of antibodies against avian influenza in European dairy cattle, the Netherlands, January 2026), we saw additional evidence of HPAI spillover into dairy cattle outside of the United States. A little over a a year ago, WOAH embraced an 11-page OFFLU technical document (see OFFLU Guidelines for High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Virus Risk Mitigation in Cattle) which - among other things - finally made HPAI in cattle a `reportable disease'. But surveillance remains passive, and testing largely up to the discretion of the livestock owner. Something that many farmers find unappealing, fearing the quarantining of their herds and the stigma of infection. Today we've an EID Journal research letter which reports compelling serological evidence not only of HPAI H5 infection in Egyptian cattle, but LPAI H9N2 as well. The authors write: Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Testing included both hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays, and positive results weren't confined to cattle. Sheep and goats tested positive for LPAI H9N2 as well. I've only posted some excerpts from this letter. Follow the link to read it in its entirety. I'll have a postscript after the break. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 Mokhtar Gomaa, Rabeh El-Shesheny, Ahmed El Taweel, Omnia Kutkat, Hager Emam, Basant Helal, Ayat Swelam, Mohamed GabAllah, Ahmed Kandeil, Pamela P. McKenzie, Richard J. Webby, Mohamed Ahmed Ali, and Ghazi Kayali Abstract Spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States sparked global concern. We investigated whether endemic avian influenza viruses are potentially spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt. We detected influenza H9N2 antibodies in 2.5% and H5N1 antibodies in 2.9%–4.5% of tested animals. Additional surveillance will elucidate host infection dynamics. (SNIP) Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus and low-pathogenicity avian influenza A(H9N2) virus are widely and endemically circulating in poultry in Egypt on farms and backyards and at live bird markets (7). Subtype H5N1 was detected in feral rats in poultry production areas (8). In addition, reassortment events between the H5N1 and H9N2 subtypes led to the emergence of novel clade 2.3.4.4b influenza A(H5N2) viruses (9). To determine whether those viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, particularly in mixed-species settings, we conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt. During October 2024–January 2026, we collected 444 serum samples from 33 conveniently selected small farms (≈10 cattle, no mixed species) and backyards housing cattle (1–3 cattle with mixed species) in 3 governorates (n = 155, n = 59, and n = 230) in northern Egypt, representing common practices in Egypt. Sheep and goats were also sampled if housed in the same backyards as cattle. All sampled animals were apparently healthy adults. We tested serum samples for antibodies against a 2025 Egyptian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (A/duck/Egypt/BA20361C/2022) virus using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays and against a G1-like Egypt influenza A(H9N2) (A/chicken/Egypt/RA20191OP/2022) virus by HI in accordance with World Health Organization protocols (10). We considered an antibody titer >1:40 as positive for both assays. Data on the number of cows, presence of other mammals (e.g., donkeys and horses), and presence of avian species (poultry and/or wild birds) were available for 271 samples. We performed statistical comparisons with χ2 or Fisher exact tests; we considered p<0.05 statistically significant. Overall, 11 (2.5%) serum specimens tested positive for influenza A(H9N2) antibodies, 20 (4.5%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by HI, and 13 (2.9%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by MN (Figure, panel A). Positive titers were 40–160 (Figure, panel B). None of the samples tested positive for antibodies against both viruses. Of the 20 H5N1 virus specimens positive by HI, 12 tested positive by MN; 1 specimen was negative by HI and positive by MN. All influenza H9N2-positive specimens were from 3 locations in the same governorate (p = 0.005). Influenza A(H5N1) antibodies were detected in 2 governorates; the differences in detection rates by governorate were statistically significant (0%, 1.3%, and 4.8%; p = 0.049). All H5N1 virus–seropositive specimens were from cattle (Table). We detected H9N2 antibodies in 6/374 (1.6%) of cattle specimens, 1/31 (3.2%) of goat specimens, and 4/39 (10.3%) of sheep specimens (p = 0.004). Presence of other animals did not predict seropositivity. Small farms had a significantly higher proportion of H5N1 virus–positive animals tested by MN (p = 0.039). Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus of the EA-2021-AB genotype and G1-like H9N2 virus appear to be spilling over into livestock in Egypt; however, because our evidence is serologic, we could not ascertain whether true infection is occurring and whether the same signs seen in the United States are common in cattle in Egypt. Even so, the evidence is a strong indicator that spillover is occurring, similar to that reported in Europe (4,6). Furthermore, spillover is not restricted to cattle; some sheep and goats tested in our study were seropositive for influenza A(H9N2) virus. Surveillance for avian influenza viruses in Egypt and other countries, especially those in which avian influenza is endemic, will verify infection and provide data on frequency, routes of transmission, and factors affecting infection of and transmission to livestock. (Continue . . . ) Despite the accrued evidence to date - for a myriad of political, societal, economic, and logistical reasons - governments around the world appear slow to respond to HPAI (and now LPAI) spillover into mammalian livestock. We see this same reluctance in investigating HPAI spillover into other species, including farmed mink (see Virological (Referral): Preliminary report on H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in Utah mink, August 2026). Although this laissez faire approach may work out in the short run, it provides these viruses with ample opportunities to spread, to evolve, and to adapt. Admittedly, most of these viruses will likely never pose a serious public health threat. But it only takes one overachiever - aided and abetted by inaction on our part - to plunge the world back into another pandemic crisis. Wednesday, November 04, 2026 NOAA Climate Prediction: West Coast Atmospheric River Event (Nov 10th-16th) NOAA Forecast Issued Nov 3rd #19,401 As we discussed 2 months ago in #NPM26: Preparing For An El Niño Winter, the west coast and the southern tier of states have been warned to expect an unusually wet and stormy winter due to the record Pacific El Niño. Predicting exactly where unusual or severe weather will occur this winter is impossible, but generally, the jet stream across the United States shifts storm tracks to the southern tier of states during an El Niño winter. Parts of Florida have already seen record flooding in the past week, but it appears that next week Northern California and the Pacific Northwest will be faced with a substantial atmospheric river event; one which could bring heavy rain and snow to much of the west coast. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center published the following warning yesterday: Key Messages from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center Issued November 2, 2026 and Updated November 3, 2026 Atmospheric River Expected to Affect the West Coast States Atmospheric river activity is expected to pull significant amounts of moisture into much of the West Coast during the second week of November and weekend, with a potential secondary moisture surge later in the period. Strong surface low pressure just north of the region will also likely drive high winds along the immediate coastline. (a) A moderate risk (40 to 60%) of heavy precipitation and possible flooding is indicated for Nov 11 to 15 across parts of the Pacific Northwest and northern/central California, while a slight risk (20 to 40%) extends to Nov 17 across the West Coast into the Desert Southwest, Great Basin, and Southern Rockies. High winds are possible across much of the West, including a moderate risk along the immediate West Coast Nov 11 to 15 and a broader slight risk extending to Nov 17. (b) A moderate risk of heavy snow is indicated across the higher elevations of the Klamath and Sierra Nevada Nov 11 to 15. Slight risks of heavy snow extend to Nov 17 for high elevations of the Cascades, Klamath, and Sierra Nevada, as well as the Northern Intermountain, Great Basin, and Central and Northern Rockies. Monitor local forecasts for safety alerts, avoid driving through flooded roadways, and use caution if traveling through high elevations. Be prepared for power outages due to high winds. This is likely just the first of many such storms expected to impact the west coast this winter, and inland freshwater flooding is a major concern. Six weeks ago, in anticipation of these events, California Declared a State of Emergency to Bolster Statewide El Niño Preparedness. The LA County website is urging both community and individual preparedness for what is expected to be a difficult winter, and advises: LA County is preparing its flood control and emergency response systems now. Crews are inspecting and maintaining dams, debris basins, channels, storm drains, and pump stations; monitoring burn areas, hillsides, and other areas at risk of flooding and debris flows; and preparing for evacuations, emergency shelter, and other storm response. County teams are also preparing to assist people experiencing homelessness, older adults, and others who may need additional help during severe weather. Here’s what residents can do now: Sign up for emergency alerts: Go to alert.lacounty.gov to receive emergency notifications, including evacuation warnings and orders. Know the risks where you live: If you are near a hillside, canyon, recent burn area, or area that can flood, learn your flood and mudflow risk before a storm. Make an evacuation plan: Know where you will go and how you will get there if you need to leave quickly. Have supplies ready: Keep enough food, water, medications, and other essentials for up to 10 days. Prepare your home: Clear gutters, downspouts, and storm drains, fix roof leaks, and get sandbags before heavy rain is in the forecast. Consider flood insurance: Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is separate and can take at least 30 days to go into effect. Need help with mud or debris flow risk? Call LA County Public Works at 1-800-933-0930 to speak with an engineer. Know someone experiencing homelessness who needs help? Visit homeless.lacounty.gov/get-help/ While this first round is expected to impact further north, now is the time for everyone along the west coast - and much of the southern United States - to prepare for severe storms and elevated flood risks. Those interested in diving into one of the more extreme (albeit, based on historic events) scenarios of Atmospheric river flooding may wish to revisit 2022's California's ARkStorm Scenario Revisited & National Preparedness Month, but even a far less severe event could be devastating. Whether it's coastal storms, inland flooding, or ice storms or tornado outbreaks in the southland, El Niño has the potential to adversely affect millions of Americans this winter (and potentially billions worldwide). So, if the power goes out today for a week, or if flood waters begin to rise . . . do you already have? A battery operated NWS Emergency Radio to find out what was going on, and to get vital instructions from emergency officials A decent first-aid kit, so that you can treat injuries Enough non-perishable food and water on hand to feed and hydrate your family (including pets) for the duration A way to provide light when the grid is down. A way to cook safely without electricity A way to purify or filter water A way to handle basic sanitation and waste disposal. A way to stay cool (fans) or warm when the power is out. A small supply of cash to use in case credit/debit machines are not working An emergency plan, including meeting places, emergency out-of-state contact numbers, a disaster buddy, and in case you must evacuate, a bug-out bag Spare supply of essential prescription medicines that you or your family may need A way to entertain yourself, or your kids, during a prolonged blackout If not, you've got some important work to do. A good place to get started is by visiting Ready.gov, or by hitting this link which will serve up a series of my preparedness blogs. When Flu Viruses Collide Antigenic `Shift' or Reassortment #19,400 Influenza co-infections in humans - or in any other susceptible host (birds, pigs, cattle, sheep, etc.) - are a public health concern because they can allow two (or more) influenza viruses to swap genetic material (reassort) and produce a hybrid virus. It's more than just a theoretical concern, as twice in my lifetime (1957 & 1968) a reassortment between seasonal flu and an avian flu virus - possibly in a human host - produced a pandemic virus. The first (1957) was pandemic H2N2, which According to the CDC emerged after three different genes from an H2N2 avian influenza A virus combined with 5 genes from the existing H1N1 virus. In 1968 a novel H3N2 virus emerged (a reassortment consisting of 2 genes from a low path avian influenza H3 virus, and 6 genes from seasonal H2N2) which continues to spark yearly epidemics more than 58 years later. While we'll never know exactly where or how these novel viruses came about, the genetic fingerprints of reassortment are unmistakable. This is the reason why yearly flu vaccination has long been recommended for people who raise pigs or work with poultry and the CDC now urges vaccination in dairy workers. Coinfection is rare, but not unheard of, and as any virologist will tell you; Shift happens. With three recent dairy-linked H5N1 cases (1 fatal) reported in Washington state - and previous evidence suggesting mild and/or asymptomatic cases may go unreported (see MMWR: Serologic Evidence of Recent Infection with HPAI A(H5) Virus Among Dairy Workers), the arrival of the fall flu season raises concerns over the possibility of seeing a rare coinfection. In addition to vaccination, the CDC also promotes (see Reducing Exposure for Workers to Avian Influenza A Viruses) the use of PPEs, but it isn't clear how many are following this advice. Since 2009, with increased surveillance and better tools, we've seen a growing number of reports of human co-infection with influenza A: EID Journal: Nosocomial Co-Transmission Of H7N9 & H1N1pdm09 EID Journal: Human Co-Infection with Avian and Seasonal Influenza Viruses, China Lancet: Coinfection With H7N9 & H3N2…

records.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, November 05, 2026 EID Journal: Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 #19,402 In the spring of 2024 a mysterious illness spreading among Texas, Kansas, and New Mexico dairy cattle was identified as avian H5N1, an outbreak that has now spread to at least 21 states, and has affected > 1200 herds. At that time cattle were believed poorly susceptible to influenza A (see A Brief History Of Influenza A In Cattle/Ruminants), and so testing for H5N1 was delayed. The immediate global reaction was that this was an `American problem', caused by a new (and presumably unique to North America) strain (B3.13) of H5N1 (see DEFRA Risk Assessment Of HPAI H5N1 Occurring in Cattle In the UK), and unlikely to occur in Europe. This strain has not been detected in the UK, and none of the viruses detected in the UK over the 2020 to 2024 HPAI outbreak period have contained genetic material originating from North or South American viruses. The risk to GB of H5N1 in livestock is assessed at very low. That assumption was challenged in June of 2024 (see Germany: FLI Statement On Experimental Infection Of Dairy Cows With European H5N1 Virus) when researchers demonstrated that a German virus isolate could replicate in a cow's udder after experimental infection. Over the summer of 2024 the USDA reassuringly suggested that B3.13 entered dairy cattle via a single spillover from birds - and was subsequently spread by the interstate transport of infected dairy cows. That assumption held until early 2025 when another genotype (D1.1) turned up in dairy cattle in two states (Nevada & Arizona). In March of 2025, the UK's Defra reported H5N1 Detected In Domestic Sheep with Mastitis, and over the previous year we'd seen reports of other non-B3.13 H5N1 in goats and sheep in Pakistan, horses in Mongolia, and pigs in Oregon. Also in the spring of 2025, Chinese scientists warned that Clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1 influenza Viruses from Birds in China Replicated Effectively in Bovine cells. Last April, in Preprint: Infection of the Bovine Mammary Gland by Avian H5N1 Subclade 2.3.4.4b Influenza viruses. we saw even more evidence that diverse HPAI H5 strains could infect dairy cattle. The authors wrote: Our findings show that mammary tissue from common cattle breeds is permissive to clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 infection. These results support the view that bovine mammary epithelium represents a susceptible tissue environment and suggest that IAV infection in cattle may be more widespread than previously assumed. Four months ago, in Eurosurveillance: Detection of antibodies against avian influenza in European dairy cattle, the Netherlands, January 2026), we saw additional evidence of HPAI spillover into dairy cattle outside of the United States. A little over a a year ago, WOAH embraced an 11-page OFFLU technical document (see OFFLU Guidelines for High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Virus Risk Mitigation in Cattle) which - among other things - finally made HPAI in cattle a `reportable disease'. But surveillance remains passive, and testing largely up to the discretion of the livestock owner. Something that many farmers find unappealing, fearing the quarantining of their herds and the stigma of infection. Today we've an EID Journal research letter which reports compelling serological evidence not only of HPAI H5 infection in Egyptian cattle, but LPAI H9N2 as well. The authors write: Our findings indicate that spillover of avian influenza viruses to cattle and other livestock is not geographically restricted or caused by certain genotypes of H5N1 virus. Testing included both hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays, and positive results weren't confined to cattle. Sheep and goats tested positive for LPAI H9N2 as well. I've only posted some excerpts from this letter. Follow the link to read it in its entirety. I'll have a postscript after the break. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Serologic Evidence of Avian Influenza Virus Exposure in Livestock, Egypt, 2024–2026 Mokhtar Gomaa, Rabeh El-Shesheny, Ahmed El Taweel, Omnia Kutkat, Hager Emam, Basant Helal, Ayat Swelam, Mohamed GabAllah, Ahmed Kandeil, Pamela P. McKenzie, Richard J. Webby, Mohamed Ahmed Ali, and Ghazi Kayali Abstract Spillover of influenza A(H5N1) virus to cattle in the United States sparked global concern. We investigated whether endemic avian influenza viruses are potentially spilling over into domestic livestock in Egypt. We detected influenza H9N2 antibodies in 2.5% and H5N1 antibodies in 2.9%–4.5% of tested animals. Additional surveillance will elucidate host infection dynamics. (SNIP) Clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus and low-pathogenicity avian influenza A(H9N2) virus are widely and endemically circulating in poultry in Egypt on farms and backyards and at live bird markets (7). Subtype H5N1 was detected in feral rats in poultry production areas (8). In addition, reassortment events between the H5N1 and H9N2 subtypes led to the emergence of novel clade 2.3.4.4b influenza A(H5N2) viruses (9). To determine whether those viruses are spilling over to livestock in Egypt, particularly in mixed-species settings, we conducted a serosurveillance study in northern Egypt. During October 2024–January 2026, we collected 444 serum samples from 33 conveniently selected small farms (≈10 cattle, no mixed species) and backyards housing cattle (1–3 cattle with mixed species) in 3 governorates (n = 155, n = 59, and n = 230) in northern Egypt, representing common practices in Egypt. Sheep and goats were also sampled if housed in the same backyards as cattle. All sampled animals were apparently healthy adults. We tested serum samples for antibodies against a 2025 Egyptian clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (A/duck/Egypt/BA20361C/2022) virus using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) and microneutralization (MN) assays and against a G1-like Egypt influenza A(H9N2) (A/chicken/Egypt/RA20191OP/2022) virus by HI in accordance with World Health Organization protocols (10). We considered an antibody titer >1:40 as positive for both assays. Data on the number of cows, presence of other mammals (e.g., donkeys and horses), and presence of avian species (poultry and/or wild birds) were available for 271 samples. We performed statistical comparisons with χ2 or Fisher exact tests; we considered p<0.05 statistically significant. Overall, 11 (2.5%) serum specimens tested positive for influenza A(H9N2) antibodies, 20 (4.5%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by HI, and 13 (2.9%) were positive for influenza A(H5N1) antibodies by MN (Figure, panel A). Positive titers were 40–160 (Figure, panel B). None of the samples tested positive for antibodies against both viruses. Of the 20 H5N1 virus specimens positive by HI, 12 tested positive by MN; 1 specimen was negative by HI and positive by MN. All influenza H9N2-positive specimens were from 3 locations in the same governorate (p = 0.005). Influenza A(H5N1) antibodies were detected in 2 governorates; the differences in detection rates by governorate were statistically significant (0%, 1.3%, and 4.8%; p = 0.049). All H5N1 virus–seropositive specimens were from cattle (Table). We detected H9N2 antibodies in 6/374 (1.6%) of cattle specimens, 1/31 (3.2%) of goat specimens, and 4/39 (10.3%) of sheep specimens (p = 0.004). Furthermore, spillover is not restricted to cattle; some sheep and goats tested in our study were seropositive for influenza A(H9N2) virus. The first (1957) was pandemic H2N2, which According to the CDC emerged after three different genes from an H2N2 avian influenza A virus combined with 5 genes from the existing H1N1 virus.
